children: Central banks may need to raise interest rates more than markets currently expect as policymakers respond to persistent inflation pressures stemming from the global energy crunch and higher oil prices, according to GlobalData TS Lombard.
The firm noted that some central banks have already tightened policy while others are expected to follow.
The current round of monetary tightening is largely a response to the surge in energy costs, which has pushed inflation further away from central banks’ targets, according to GlobalData TS Lombard.

While policymakers would typically look through supply-side shocks and the temporary inflation pressures they create, five years of above-target inflation has made such an approach increasingly difficult.
The firm said fragile private-sector inflation expectations could become unanchored unless central banks demonstrate a firm commitment to their statutory price-stability objectives.

Markets, however, are pricing in only a moderate degree of additional tightening, with expectations for less than 100 basis points of rate increases. GlobalData TS Lombard said that measured response makes sense as an initial reaction to the global energy crisis, particularly because labor markets have cooled and a significant second-round inflation effect is unlikely.
At the same time, the firm believes markets may be underestimating the extent of monetary tightening that could ultimately be required, particularly from the Federal Reserve.
The key risk to the current market view is a stronger-than-expected U.S. labor market, GlobalData TS Lombard said.

The firm is bullish on U.S. employment prospects and argued that if payroll growth meets its expectations over the next 12 months, the resulting strength in labor demand could push the eventual terminal interest rate significantly higher than currently anticipated.
Stronger employment would also raise questions about whether monetary policy is actually as restrictive as the Federal Reserve believes.
GlobalData TS Lombard added that stronger labor demand could have another important consequence by dampening expectations for productivity gains linked to artificial intelligence.

If robust employment growth persists while AI-related productivity improvements fail to materialize as quickly as expected, policymakers could face less justification for assuming that productivity will offset inflationary pressures.

As a result, the firm sees a risk that the eventual path for interest rates, especially in the U.S., could be considerably higher than the less-than-100-basis-point tightening currently priced by markets.

title: Central banks may need to raise rates more than markets expect: TS Lombard
